extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IPR parties, patent examiners, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for evaluating patent claim invalidity (anticipation under §102 and obviousness under §103) in an inter partes review, drawing on Graham, KSR, and Federal Circuit precedent. Focuses on what prior art must show (single-reference disclosure or motivation/expectation to combine) and evidentiary proof requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of obviousness is resolved on the basis of underlying factual determinations including: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) any differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness. Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 17–18 (1966).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four factual determinations as the framework for any §103 analysis; consider objective/secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt need) as part of the fourth factor. KSR further explains that courts may account for inferences and creative steps a person of ordinary skill would employ when applying these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: When all elements of a claim are found in various pieces of prior art, the factfinder must consider whether a person of ordinary skill in the art would be motivated to combine those references, and whether in making that combination, a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success. Dome Patent L.P. v. Lee, 799 F.3d 1372, 1380 (Fed. Cir. 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A §103 challenge based on multiple references requires affirmative proof both of a suggestion/motivation to combine and of a reasonable expectation of success in doing so. Look to the references, not hindsight, for evidence of motivation/expectation. Case law (WMS Gaming; Concrete Pipe) emphasizes the need for some suggestion or motivation in the prior art to combine references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion/motivation and expectation must be founded in prior art, not applicant's disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Both the suggestion and the expectation of success must be founded in the prior art, not in the applicant’s disclosure." In re Dow Chemical Co., 837 F.2d 469, 473 (Fed. Cir. 1988).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that rely on the patent specification or the patentee's own work to supply the reason to combine or the expectation of success are improper. The rationale for combining references and any claimed predictability must be supported by the prior art record.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR 'obvious to try' and predictable-solution context
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention may be found obvious if trying a course of conduct would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art: when there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options within his or her technical grasp. KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 421 (2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply KSR where the art points to a limited set of predictable solutions and market/design pressures would prompt a skilled artisan to pursue them; but also ensure that the combination is more than the predictable use of prior art elements (see Kubin). KSR permits considering ordinary creativity and common sense, not hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires every element in a single reference (express or inherent)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim to be anticipated, each claim element must be disclosed, either expressly or inherently, in a single prior art reference, and the claimed arrangement or combination of those elements must also be disclosed, either expressly or inherently, in that same prior art reference. Therasense, Inc. v. Becton, Dickinson and Co., 593 F.3d 1325, 1332–33 (Fed. Cir. 2010); Sanofi‑Synthelabo v. Apotex, Inc., 550 F.3d 1075, 1082 (Fed. Cir. 2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation is a strict, four-corners test: every limitation must be found in a single prior art reference. Where an element is not expressly disclosed, analyze whether it is inherently disclosed (see inherency standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency standard for anticipation: 'necessarily present' / 'unavoidably teaches'
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference may anticipate inherently if a claim limitation that is not expressly disclosed 'is necessarily present, or inherent, in the single anticipating reference.' The very essence of inherency is that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize that a reference unavoidably teaches the property in question. Verizon Servs. Corp. v. Cox Fibernet Va., Inc., 602 F.3d 1325, 1337 (Fed. Cir. 2010); Agilent Techs., Inc. v. Affymetrix, Inc., 567 F.3d 1366, 1383 (Fed. Cir. 2009).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherency requires inevitability — the missing limitation must be necessarily present, not merely possible or likely. If the reference allows alternative implementations that would not include the limitation (e.g., multiple injections instead of a single-device 162 mg dose), inherency is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the challenged claims are unpatentable under the asserted statutory grounds (e.g., 35 U.S.C. § 102 for anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All factual and legal assertions about what the prior art discloses, public accessibility of a reference, motivation to combine, and expectation of success must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement must be more than predictable use of prior art elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 103 bars patentability unless 'the improvement is more than the predictable use of prior art elements according to their established functions.' In re Kubin, 561 F.3d 1351, 1359–60 (Fed. Cir. 2009) (citing KSR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting obviousness, the combination should not merely reflect routine optimization or use of known elements performing their established functions unless there is a reason in the prior art to do so that renders the combination obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction principle: do not import limitations from the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should not be limited by reciting unclaimed specifics from the specification (e.g., importing a particular disease into a claim that does not recite it). Acceleration Bay, LLC v. Activision Blizzard Inc., 908 F.3d 765, 771 (Fed. Cir. 2018).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating prior art or claim scope, assess the claim language itself; avoid reading examples or preferred embodiments in the specification into the claim unless the claim expressly includes those limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of public accessibility for online records (e.g., ClinicalTrials.gov)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that an online record was publicly accessible on a given date, declarations and evidence must credibly show how the record could be located and accessed (search parameters, qualifications of declarant), and address existence of other registries or non-standardized search behaviors that might affect accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations relying solely on locating a study by its identifier (e.g., NCT number) without showing how a person of ordinary skill would have found it via ordinary searches may be insufficient. Show who performed the search, their qualifications, the search terms/parameters used, and explain why the record would have been findable to the public on the critical date; account for alternative registries and non-standardized drug/condition names.
